citation: 'Famous Homes' [the Philip D. Armour residence, 2115 Prairie Avenue]. Halftone photograph with caption, Chicago Sunday Tribune, 8 July 1928 (vol. 87, no. 28); Tribune photo.
author: Chicago Tribune (Tribune photo)
repository: Internet Archive, Chicago Tribune microfilm, item per_chicago-daily-tribune_1928-07-08_87_28, page index 97; the Prairie library's image nps-2115-tribune-1928-07-08-famous-homes-photo (stream-newspapers-south), held in the image store.
locator: The photograph of the house front and the caption under it.
rights_note: A photograph published in a US newspaper in 1928, before 1929: public domain in the United States. Read for forms only; no asset is derived from it.
access_notes: Read 2026-10-19 (T-2642) from the image store's copy, 1223 x 1400 px, sha256 e7a6cf89a2d7c814cd804c860b6035d403633b336d6855d47a45aa3b8a9309d7; the caption read on the same copy.
note: The caption: 'The old 19-room stone residence of Philip D. Armour, founder of the packing firm of Armour & Co., was a show place in its day. Now used as a rooming house, it still stands at 2115 Prairie avenue.' The photograph is dark but shows the front: two storeys with round-arched windows, a tall mansard storey above them with round-headed dormers, iron cresting along the top of the mansard between tall corner stacks, and a straight flight of steps up to the door in the middle. It shows the house in 1928, twenty-four years after the 1904 scene.
what_it_supplies: that the house was of stone and still stood in 1928
the front's mansard, dormers, round-arched windows, cresting and front steps as photographed in 1928
what_it_does_not_supply: the 1904 state: nothing on the front is recorded as changed, but nothing says it was not
the year the house came down
